utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. I'm told the parties wish to make a submission on documents. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, and we have a submission according to the events that happened on Friday, and on suggestion of Mr. Tom Hannis, my learned colleague from the Prosecutor's side, as at this point, he's not sure whether this is under any protective measures, we would suggest jointly that it's done in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're talking about material which is to be referred to which may be the subject of protective --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is this material which has already been referred to or has yet to be referred to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is -- it has been referred to, but now we're talking about the specific material, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. And you wish to go into private session for the moment to deal with this, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We shall go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours. [The witness entered court].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor Markovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've had an administrative matter to deal with, that explains the brief delay; but you will be no doubted pleased to know that as a result you've been vindicated, and we've been advised that you did, unknown to the parties here, have access to the stenographic notes of the meetings of the SDC between October 1997 and March 1999, at least the ones for which there were stenographic notes. We know that in one case there are no notes, and it may be there were no notes for two of them. However, that was a matter that we were discussing and have resolved, and Mr. Hannis will now continue with his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor. When we finished on Friday, we were talking about the Supreme Defence Council and their meetings. And I know you testified last week, I think on Tuesday, that based on your review of those nine meetings between October 1997 and March of 1999, that you saw no instance of a document entitled, "Decision of the Supreme Defence Council," correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I guess my question to you is: Is there a reason that the word "decisions" in reference to the Supreme Defence Council and how they work, is there any reason that we have to give that something other than the non-generic meaning of "decisions"? Does it say anywhere that those kinds of decisions have to be published?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the constitution says that for regulations in general enactments must be published before they can take effect. Only then do they acquire legal power. Without being published, they have no legal effect. I quoted an article -- I quoted a position of the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia which refused to review the constitutionality of a decision by the then-president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia because the conditions -- preconditions had not been met for the constitutionality of that decision, and the enactment itself had never been published; therefore, it was not subject to a revision of its constitutionality or legality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With regard to the rules of procedure for the Supreme Defence Council, I think Exhibit P22 -- or 2622 are the rules from 1992 and Exhibit P1738 are the rules from March of 1999. I see nothing in the rules of procedure that require decisions or conclusions of the SDC to be published. There is nothing in their own rules of procedure about that, is there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This sort of thing is not something that is normally enshrined in the book of rules or the rules of procedure. As far as the general enactments and regulations being published, this is something for the constitution to deal with, not for any rules of procedure. There cannot be a regulation or an enactment with legal force that has not been published in the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, Professor, that there is an argument to be made that given the nature of this body, the Supreme Defence Council, made up of the highest -- some of the highest-ranking individuals in the country, the president of the Republic of Yugoslavia and the presidents of the two member republics, as well as the Chief of the General Staff of the army, and the kinds -- the subject matter that they talked about, the use of the army, defence of the country, that those oftentimes would involve sensitive matters that should not be subject to publication?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, but there is also an official military gazette. The Official Gazette of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was not the only one; besides, I don't know how a provision on the responsibility of the president of the republic for violations of the constitution can be implemented if he does not act in compliance with the Supreme Defence Council, if he fails to exercise command over the army in compliance with decisions by the Supreme Defence Council for as long as we don't know what the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council actually are. It seems that the president is immune from responsibility, at least as far as this issue is concerned, which is exercising command over the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a general question about that. In the former Yugoslavia, in Serbia, were there any laws or statutory provisions about state secrets? I understand that General Perisic at one time was subject of some kind of prosecution in Serbia for a violation of disclosing state secrets, something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is certainly such a thing as a state secret and there are laws governing this issue, but, believe me, I'm not familiar with those particular regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, one of the things I wasn't clear about regarding how the Supreme Defence Council worked in -- well, prior to the rule changes in March 1999, did it require a consensus? Did everyone have to agree -- or I think there's a provision that talks about that the Supreme Defence Council can conduct its work when it has a majority of members present. And if that's the case, does it only require agreement of those present as opposed to unanimity of all the members? That wasn't a very elegant question, but I hope you can understand it.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the question. I agree with you. There's a provision in the 1992 rules of procedure -- there is no provision in the 1992 rules of procedure on how decisions are taken, but the Supreme Defence Council can continue to operate, even if only as many as or as few as two of its members are present. It would seem to follow that no consensus is required to pass decisions; the majority will do. Although, I personally believe that the council, as a collective, body does not exist if all of its three members are not present. There is a legal saying in Latin, "tres faciunt collegium." It takes three members to make up a collective body; however, the rules of procedure clearly say the council can continue to work as long as two of its members are present. However, if you interpret this systematically, the void can be filled indeed the following way: One can, for example, establish that the council can pass decisions by a majority vote of those members who are actually present, which means that the presence of two of its members are required for -- in order for a majority to be accomplished. But this remained valid until the 3rd of March, 1999. From there on, there was a consensus procedure in place, and there had to be unanimity on the part of all the members of the council.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So my -- my understanding then is prior to March 23rd, 1999, of the three members, a meeting can be held and business could be had if only the two of the three members were present, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That seems to follow from a particular rule in the rules of procedure governing the work of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if two members, say, President Milutinovic and President Milosevic, were present, they can conduct business and reach conclusions and take decisions that would be valid under your understanding of the Supreme Defence Council, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, this is not just my interpretation. That's what the rules actually state, the rules governing the work of the Supreme Defence Council, and you read that decision, too. The Supreme Defence Council may continue to work, even when one of its members are not present, under the 1992 rules of procedure. That was the first time this rule was envisaged, and Mr. Dobrica Cosic was the president then. That's when the rules were adopted. What this also means is that two votes is all it takes for a decision to be adopted. One no longer needs three votes because, after all, the council can be convened with only two of its members in attendance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In your review of those nine meetings between October 1997 and March 1999, did you see any occasion where President Milutinovic disagreed or voted against President Milosevic's position on anything?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Milutinovic only started attending sessions early in 1998. There was always unanimity except when the Chief of the General Staff was replaced. The three members would always agree except when it came to replacing the Chief of the General Staff. Mr. Milo Djukanovic opposed this decision, but this wasn't something for the Supreme Defence Council to rule upon. This followed from Article 136 of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In addition to that, the one time where you say President Djukanovic disagreed about the replacement of General Perisic, do you also recall the meeting of the Supreme Defence Council in December 1998, where President Djukanovic raised an issue about the promotion or the appointment of General Pavkovic to be commander of the 3rd Army, and he based that objection partly on information he had, suggesting that while General Pavkovic had been commander of the Pristina Corps, that body of the army had engaged in some allegedly unconstitutional activity in Kosovo. Do you recall that from your review?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that he had certain objections that he did not state very strenuously, but I don't think the reasons actually boiled down to what you defined them as. I think we should look up the minutes to check.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We can do that. Let me see if I can find the reference to that exhibit and tab number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may be of help, it's tab 57. Exhibit is P1000.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. I should know that one by heart.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as I recall, Professor, I think that discussion came in the last two pages of those minutes, if that helps. I think it's probably on -- it begins on page 14 of your version and the next-to-last page of the English. Well, maybe even we have to go back one page further to catch the very beginning of President Djukanovic's remarks. Yes. Page 9 of the English. I think, Professor, he speaks right after General Ojdanic had spoken, and it's on page 13 of your version and it's three pages from the end.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think it's in the third paragraph under his name.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, in English, I'm reading the second line, where it says: "However, he did draw attention to the conflicting information coming from Kosovo in recent months regarding the involvement of the Pristina Corps. Information coming from Montenegro was often such that it indicated the Pristina Corps's actions were not always in accordance with the constitutional role of the army and the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council." Does that refresh your recollection about what his objection --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I wonder if we can go to the next page. It seems that President Milosevic just denied that there had been any problem; but below that, President Milutinovic speaks and it says he added that: "Some reports of alleged lack of discipline and unconstitutional actions by the Pristina Corps were usually 'inflated.'" Now, Professor, I read that to mean that President Milutinovic seems to be suggesting that, yes, there were reports about that, but usually they were inflated, overexaggerated, I take it. Doesn't that suggest that President Milutinovic seems to be indicating that, yes, there were some reports about that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this paragraph cannot really be interpreted properly without reading the previous paragraph. The previous paragraph reads that: "There had been certain shortcomings in the preparation for this session because the proposals, including the proposal for General Pavkovic, were not accompanied by listings." Then he instructed General Ojdanic, it says, to present to the members of the council those listings from his own background material. President Djukanovic, after reviewing these documents, stated that it was quite sufficient. I believe that, in view of what was written in the listings and the remark of Mr. Djukanovic that it was quite sufficient, the sentence uttered by the President of the Republic of Serbia, Mr. Milan Milutinovic, is to be read within that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, Professor. Thank you. At that time, though, in December of 1998, before there was a change in the rules of procedure, it really didn't matter how strong President Djukanovic's objections might have been. The simple fact is that, if President Milutinovic voted with Mr. Milosevic, President Djukanovic was going to be out-voted every time, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In theory, yes; but in practice, that happened only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you would agree with me, I guess, when we're discussing in general terms Mr. Milutinovic's powers as a president of the Republic of Serbia, because of the fact that he possesses one vote of the three votes owned by the Supreme Defence Council, that gives him a certain amount of power, because on a controversial issue his vote will be the swing vote and decide whether or not a particular decision or conclusion will be taken or not, agreed?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not have any powers of the kind you suggest regarding controversial issues. On the basis of his membership in the Supreme Defence Council, he did not have any powers, just as Mr. Djukanovic. He was just a member taking part in the discussions and in the voting, no more. And at all sessions, whose stenographic notes or minutes I have read, we see that unanimity existed always, except in that one case. And sessions of the Supreme Defence Council no longer took place from March 1999 until October 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But you would agree with me, as a general principle, it's fair to say that, for example, if I were a member of the Presidency of the -- I guess, it was the SFRY, when there was still eight members, six republics and two autonomous provinces, having one of eight votes doesn't give me as much control or power as having one of three votes, correct? Just in general.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Only the Presidency worked on the principle of consensus, so that even one vote alone could deadlock the Presidency. On the level of speculation, you are completely right. What you're saying is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, and that's a very point, too, Professor. It makes a difference about whether we're talking about a body where the decision has to be taken unanimously or by a majority. That does make a difference But in the example we talked about, the replacement of General Perisic, if President Milutinovic had decided to side with President Djukanovic, that could have called for a different result, wouldn't it? Or is it your position that President Milosevic in those circumstances could do whatever he wanted anyway?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Milosevic had constitutional powers, according to Article 136, to decide on the issue alone, independently. And I don't understand why he included the issue in the agenda at all, in the agenda of the Supreme Defence Council, that is. He didn't even need to seek the opinion of the two others. He just wanted to hear their opinion; otherwise, he would not have been in violation of the constitution even if he had taken the decision on his own, without asking the opinion of the two other members.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question about Article 136, then, that you refer to. I recall there's a provision in there that says: "Stipulated by law." What is that referring to? That seemed to be some sort of limitation on the president's power, on President Milosevic's power under Article 136. Do you know the one I'm referring to, or should we pull up the document?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what you mean. Well, promotions, appointments, and dismissals up to the level of colonel and including the level of colonel were carried out by the Chief of General Staff. As far as generals are concerned, appointments, promotions, and recalls were the purview of the president of Yugoslavia. So that article, 136, of the constitution should be read in conjunction with the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia, because that is the law that is meant in the reference made to the law in Article 136.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is there any provision in the Law on the Army about the replacement of the Chief of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the issue of the appointment of the Chief of General Staff falls precisely within the jurisdiction of the president of the republic. That is his constitutional responsibility and power according to Article 136 of the constitution. He is the one who issues the ordinance on appointment, not the SDC.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you about one other provision of the rules of procedure for the SDC in 1998 and early 1999. I think it's Article 7 that seems to indicate that the SDC can also conduct its work without actually having a session, but by having consultation among the members. Are you familiar with that provision?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with the provision, and it is contained in the rules of procedure dating from 1992 and later 2001, but I believe the 1999 rules of procedure did not contain it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I -- that's something I'm not clear about. The 1999 rules of procedure made specific reference to the fact that they were modifying, I think, Articles 3 and 4 of the 1992 rules, correct? I think it said Articles 3 and 4 of the 1992 rules are hereby specifically annulled or voided, something to that effect, right? Exhibit P1738 are the 1999 rules, and I'm sorry I don't have the tab number. I think it's tab number 60 for you, Professor, 6-0.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I've forgotten your question. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the new 1999 rules, isn't a specific reference to the fact that there intended to withdraw or annul or revoke something - I don't have it in front of me - Articles 3 and 4 of the 1992 rules? I think it's at the -- near the end?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is the last. It's Article 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 10 says: "The rules of procedure of the SDC becomes null and void in its entirety," not only Articles 1 and 3. It is just that it was referenced as number 1-3, dated 23rd March 1999. The whole rules of procedure were voided. You see, the current rules of procedure that we are looking at are referenced as 3-4. It says: "Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Supreme Defence Council, number 3-4, Belgrade," et cetera. So the whole rules of procedure become null and void.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm confused about the reference to numbers in Article 10. Article 10, in English -- sorry. Mr. Zecevic, can you clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think, Your Honours, the -- there is a problem with the transcript. It refers to 1 and 3, and Professor was saying 3 and 4 all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that creates the confusion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Articles 1 and 3, I said, are not important. All articles of the previous rules of procedure become null and void, and new rules of procedure, including ten articles, enter into force. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There seems to be a substitution of one for the other here, because at the beginning of the rules we are looking at for 1999, they are said to be Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Supreme Defence Council, number 1-3, and the Professor has called this 3-4 so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Professor is referring to the previous tab, 59, which is a document of 1992. The rules of procedure of 1992 have the number 3-4; and by the rules of 1999, the previous -- the previous rules of procedure with a number 3-4 of 20 -- of July 1992 has ceased to exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. That clarifies it, Mr. Zecevic. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And for the record, I think, tab 59 is Exhibit P2622.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, Professor, thank you for clearing that up. And I think a couple of times you mentioned that you weren't certain why some of these matters regarding personnel, for example, were put on the agenda for discussion at the SDC, because your view is that under, I think, Article 135 and/or 136 of the constitution, President Milosevic could by himself make those decisions. He did not need any input from the SDC, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But under the rules of procedure in 1998, before the change in March 1999, isn't the president of the Republic of Yugoslavia, President Milosevic, wasn't he the one who set the agenda, scheduled the agenda?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the one who decided on the agenda, what would be included. And at the session where the Chief of General Staff was replaced, he said that in future, regardless of the fact that the issue was in his jurisdiction, he would always consult the Supreme Defence Council. That's the minutes from the November 1998 session where the Chief of General Staff was replaced. It's towards the end of the minutes in a contribution by President Milosevic, when he was interpreting Articles 135 and 136 and the relationship of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia towards the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There's certainly -- and there's certainly nothing in the constitution or the law or the rules of procedure of the SDC that prevents him from soliciting input from the other members of the SDC about personnel matters, such as promotions and appointments, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was under no obligation to seek anyone's opinion, just as with the appointment of judges and so-called jury judges and military prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand he had no obligation, but there was no prohibition from seeking their input; and as a matter of fact, it seems to make good sense and be a good practice to get input from some of your top advisors on an issue like that; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Anyone who was authorised to make decisions was able and authorised to consult others, including experts, in order to make the right decision; however, the constitution imposed no such obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, at page 13030, on the 8th of August, you were talking about the Supreme Defence Council, and you said based on your review it seemed that they were inclined to include in its agenda matters that were not within its realm of work at all. My question is to you: Who decides what the realm of work of the SDC is?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is broadly outlined in the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, where it says that the Army of Yugoslavia is commanded by the president of Yugoslavia, in keeping with the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council. It follows, therefrom, that the main and only jurisdiction of the Supreme Defence Council is to command the Army of Yugoslavia, and the Law on Defence also specifies the specific powers of the SDC, item by item. I believe it's in Article 4, if I'm not mistaken, on the Law on Defence. And anything that is not on that list of powers of the SDC is not in its jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But commanding the army of a country like Yugoslavia is a big job, and President Milosevic, as the supreme commander with ultimate responsibility, and also as being the person who sets the agenda for the SDC, it seems that he would have a lot of discretion in deciding what matters need to be discussed by the SDC to assist him in knowing how to do his job and what to do in commanding the army. Wouldn't you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with that; although, those were powers quite usual and normal for a head of state. In most countries of the world, the head of state is simultaneously the supreme commander of the armed forces, and he has those powers by virtue of the fact that he is head of state.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, Professor. At page 13033, you were talking about the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council, as referenced by President Djukanovic in one of those minutes, and you said: "Yes, but what are these decisions of the Supreme Defence Council that President Djukanovic has in mind? Nowhere were any such decisions published. There are no such decisions. He probably means positions. Positions, that's probably what he means because everybody says that positions are taken by the Supreme Council. Positions are not decisions in a formal sense." Let me ask you this: Have you ever talked to President Djukanovic to ask him what he meant when he said "decisions" in the context of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So, in fairness, you're only speculating about what he might have meant, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you would agree with me that Mr. Djukanovic, as president of the Republic of Montenegro, was in a position to have some notion of what a decision is, that being president of Montenegro must involve making lots of decisions?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly he had some notion of what a decision is; although, I'm not quite sure, in view of the fact that Mr. Djukanovic is not a lawyer, that he was aware what a decision should look like in formal terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I understand the point that I believe you were making about that. Is it correct that your position is that the lack of publication meant that these weren't decisions in a formal legalistic sense?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. Not only were they not published, they were not adopted because we can see from the stenographic record that only conclusions were adopted. The stenographic records would have had to register a decision being adopted; whereas, they mention only conclusions. As we have seen, these conclusions are not formulated as legal norms, but as political positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question about that. I know in another case I worked on reviewing some legislative materials from -- I think from the Republika Srpska, Assembly decisions and maybe Crisis Staff meeting documents, that oftentimes I would see perhaps in the same document or appended together there would be something that was first called a conclusion, and then there would be either a decree or a decision. Is that -- isn't that the case, that often a conclusion precedes a decree or a decision?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as I said, I don't know, but I've never seen a decision or decree of the Supreme Council. I doubt that they were able to issue decrees. Like the president of the republic and the Chief of the General Staff, they could issue orders, rules, instructions, decisions, of course, but not decrees; because, as we have seen, it was the cabinet that issued decrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But with regard to -- I guess my question is as a general matter. Is it fair to say that sometimes a formal sort of document called "conclusions" would -- would be issued as sort of a preliminary or antecedent document for something called a "decision," because it seems to be -- it shows the body has deliberated a particular matter, concluded something about the situation, and then made a decision object what should be done based on those conclusions, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's correct, because a conclusion is a basis for a decision. Conclusions contain standpoints, and they have to be shaped to become legal norms. And I think that this is all in compliance with the name of the body. This body is called a "council," so its purpose is more to give advice, counsel, on which decisions can be based, rather than issuing decisions itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, Professor, that the lack of publication of any decisions does not mean that real -- real-world, non-formal substantive decisions weren't ever taken by the Supreme Defence Council, does it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you. Such decisions had to be made, but they were not published, at least to the best of my knowledge, as far as I was able to ascertain by inspecting the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we look at Exhibit P1574.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I'll try and find the tab number for you, Professor. These are the minutes of the 9th of June. That's tab 54 I think in your grey binder. It's the minutes of the 5th Session of the Supreme Defence Council on the 9th of June, 1998, and I think you probably recall this one, Professor. You know that one of the conclusions taken from this meeting was that if terrorist activities of the Albanian separatist movement escalated, the Yugoslav Army will, I think, intervene adequately; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the second conclusion from this session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Explain for me the difference between "conclusion" and "decision" in that context, because in non-generic terms, to me, that seems to be a decision; that if a certain contingency occurs, then the army is going to intervene adequately. We don't know what the details of what that is, because I assume that will vary depending on the nature and degree of the escalation, but how is that conclusion different from a generic decision?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the Army of Yugoslavia to be able to intervene "adequately," as it says here, what is necessary is that this decision should be made operational. The "Army of Yugoslavia" is a very general term. It's an overarching term. Is it the entire army or a certain corps? Well, I'm no expert on military matters, but you cannot see who in the Army of Yugoslavia should intervene, where they should intervene, and to what extent. What does "adequate" mean here?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Earlier, though, in your testimony on Tuesday last week, you had said about the Supreme Defence Council that the only -- from your review, they only adopted conclusions of a political nature and not of a military or professional nature. Isn't this a military conclusion, to the extent that it calls for engagement of the army?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All the conclusions had to do with the army and the military matters, but the way in which they were formulated was couched in political terms. It was political language, the language of a political body. They all had to do, the conclusions I mean, with military matters and the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, did you have any chance to review any VJ General Staff or Supreme Command Staff documents to see if there were any references therein to SDC decisions?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not have an opportunity to see such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So, if I understand correctly, you're saying that the SDC was just issuing conclusions or positions on matters. If that's the case -- and the conclusions weren't published either, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. The conclusions weren't published either. They are an integral part of the minutes, as is the stenographic record. The minutes were not available to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So I -- so what is the purpose then of having conclusions, to what end, if nobody knows about them except those guys meeting?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose is what the conclusions say. They are addressed, as a rule, to the Army of Yugoslavia. That was the purpose of the conclusions. All the conclusions have to do exclusively with the Army of Yugoslavia, including those from the session of, I think, the 4th of October, the 4th of October, 1998, which say that if the country is attacked, it will be defended by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, then you would agree that some things were done as a result of these conclusions reached by the SDC, correct? The army must have taken some sort of action based on these conclusions.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. But what I'm saying is that between the action and the conclusion, there had to be some sort of document in between; whether a legal enactment, a general one, or an act of command, I don't know, because I've never seen one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next then could we go to Exhibit P2166. Now, Professor, I don't know if you've seen this one before or not. I think it was on the 65 ter list. Yes, I see it's tab number 49, I think, in your grey binder, 49. And this is a document from the 2nd of November, 1998, reporting about -- it's actually the minutes of a meeting that occurred on the 29th of October, 1998. Do you find that one in your binder, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Looking at it now, do you recall if you had a chance to see it before while preparing for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you want to take a couple of minute to look at it. It's a long document. I'm not going to go through the whole thing, but my questions will relate to the first three pages, if you want to have a look at that before I start asking them.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Yes. I'm sure that I have not had these minutes in my hands before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You'll see it's describing the minutes of a group called the "Operations Inter-Departmental Staff for the Suppression of Terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija," correct? That's what my English says; is that --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When you translate it into Serbian, it's the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of such a body before?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is there any provision in the constitution for that kind of body?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We have seen that there are several provisions, six articles, but no such body is mentioned in the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, we see that the meeting was chaired by President Milosevic, and then it lists those attending, and we see several politicians, I think, four army generals and one, two, three, four police generals from the Ministry of Interior. There is one individual, though, that does not appear to be a member of the government or the police and the army, and that's Dusan Matkovic. He's listed as the vice-president of the Socialist Party of Serbia, the SPS. Did you know Mr. Matkovic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he hold any position in the government in 1998, that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in 1998. But in the first Government of the Republic of Serbia, I think he was -- no. I'm sure he was a minister, but I don't recall what for, whether industry or something else. I'm not sure what his portfolio was, but I'm sure he was a minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, as far as the other political persons in attendance, do you know what party they were a member of? Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Milutinovic, Mr. Minic, and Mr. Sainovic were all members of the SPS, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that was a party that you were a member of in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in the second paragraph, you'll see that Mr. Milosevic opened the session and informed the members about the agenda, indicated that Generals Pavkovic and Lukic were going to speak, followed by Mr. Minic, and that General Pavkovic was going to present the proposals of the Joint Command. And you see that in capital letters, at least it's in capital letters in my English. Do you know what the Joint Command was?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me have you go to page 3, and I think the B/C/S and the English are in harmony in this instance. It's about four paragraphs up from the bottom, and it's underlined, I think. In the English, it reads: "Pursuant to the Decision adopted at the 5th Session of the Supreme Defence Council on 9 June 1998 ..." You see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you read it out for us, please, so I can be sure our English is correct on the written version?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. This is what it says: "Pursuant to the Decision adopted at the 5th Session of the Supreme Defence Council held on the 9th of June, 1998, the Law on the Yugoslav Army, the Law on Defence, and the rules of service of the Army of Yugoslavia, a plan to suppress terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija was drawn up, which provided for the engagement of units of the MUP of Serbia and the Army of Yugoslavia." There are only two typographical errors. In the words "plan," there is an inversion of the letters; and instead of "terrorism," it says "terrotism." So these are evidently typographical errors.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you are satisfied that it is intended to mean plan to suppress terrorism, even though "plan" and "terrorism" appear to be misspelled?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's quite clear. It's evidently just a typographical error.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in my English version, it says: "Pursuant to the Decision." "Decision" is in a capital "D"; and, to me, that means it has the non-generic meaning, some sort of specific, formal legal meaning. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what it should mean, as you say. If there's a capital letter, then it must be the title of a particular document. Had it been lower case "d," for decision, it would have had a general meaning. But if it's capitalised, then it's the title of a specific document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But in the rules and the laws and the constitutional provisions about the SDC taking decisions, isn't "decision" with a small "d" in all those other places?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Decisions are with a small "d" because decisions can have different titles, but their essence is that some kind of decision is made in them. They themselves can probably bear different titles; and as I said, the nomenclature of the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council was never regulated, what kinds of decisions it was able to adopt.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, this would seem to indicate that, even though we didn't see it in the minutes of that June 9th, 1998 meeting, that indeed a decision was taken by the Supreme Defence Council. Would you agree, just reading this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what follows from this paragraph, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And among the persons attending this October 29th meeting of the Operations Inter-Departmental Staff are Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Milutinovic, and General Perisic, who were all at that 9 June meeting of the SDC, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I know you haven't had a chance to look through the whole document, Professor, but I would indicate to you that I saw nothing to suggest that any of those attendees at the SDC meeting interrupted General Pavkovic or later on corrected him and said, "Wait, wait, wait. We didn't take any decision on June 9th." Will you accept my representation about that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I hope you've read it through carefully. Probably you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, if I haven't, I'm sure one of my friends across the way would bring it to my attention and your attention as well. So, even though prior to today you haven't had a chance to see anything indicating the Supreme Defence Council took decisions, this document would indicate that there was at least one occasion where they, indeed, did, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here; although, one cannot see from this where that decision might be, whether it was published anywhere. It's not an integral part of the minutes. We've just had a look at that session. We didn't see this. We saw only three very general conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And in fairness to you, Professor, I note that this document, Exhibit P2166, is stamped "State Secret." So that may, in part, explain why that decision of the Supreme Defence Council was not published, because we're talking about sort of secret things we don't want the general public, and certainly we don't want the terrorists or the so-called KLA to know about, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. The word "secret" is included, especially as in state secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me move off of that one then, Professor, and go to another related topic. Mr. Zecevic was asking you about how decisions and orders were implemented within the army, and you talked about -- you began talking about regulations and how regulations needed to be published because the constitution says that all regulations need to be published. This is at page 13045 of the transcript. And I understand the sense of that that it's not fair to punish somebody for ignorance of the law. If you don't know about a regulation, then you certainly shouldn't be published. But can you explain the difference for us between a decision, an order, and a regulation?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Law on the Army does not define these acts, such as, for example, the Law on the Government which defines all the enactments defined by the government. It doesn't specify what these enactments are. As to the nature of these enactments and the depth of relations that they define, the Law on the Army says nothing about those; therefore, I myself am unable to shed any light on that. Perhaps a military expert might be able to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, Professor. Following on that discussion, you mentioned "The president," and this is at page 13046. You mentioned that: "The president of the republic cannot be held responsible for violating the constitution if he were to command without the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council, because we don't know at all whether the Supreme Defence Council has issued any decisions and where these decisions were published." Now, we talked about the possibility that because of the nature of the subject matter, it might be important not to publish those decisions and keep them secret; but would you allow, Professor, for the possibility that you might have, in these circumstances, a president of the republic, Mr. Milosevic, who didn't want to be held responsible for violating the constitution?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what exactly you mean. He didn't want to be held responsible. Well, no president ever wants to be held responsible for violating the constitution. If that is established, his term of office is at an end. Each president always does his best to act in compliance with the constitution; therefore, I don't think I really understand your question well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I guess part of my confusion stems from a little further on. On page 13046, you say, beginning at line 6: "So, according to the 1992 constitution, the president of the republic could command, even without the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council, without violating the constitution. Why? Because we have no such decisions of the Supreme Defence Council, and we do not know whether he commanded in accordance with those decisions or not; and who formulated those decisions, we don't know that either." Could you explain that for me, because I'm not sure what that means: Because we have no decisions, we can't know what they were. So whatever the president does cannot be held as violative of the constitution, because we don't know what the Supreme Defence Council did?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I believe. If you look at Article 135, paragraph 1 of the constitution, it says that it is the president of the republic who exercises command over the army, both in peace and wartime, in keeping with decisions taken by the Supreme Defence Council; therefore, the command exercised by the president of the republic must remain in compliance with any decisions taken by the Supreme Defence Council. Should he fail to exercise command in compliance with any decisions taken by the Supreme Defence Council, that would constitute a violation of the constitution. Under Article 97, paragraph 7 of the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the president of the republic can be recalled only if the Federal Assembly establishes that he has violated the constitution. How can we know if the president of the republic exercises command over the Army of Yugoslavia, both in peace and wartime, in keeping with any decisions taken by the Supreme Defence Council, if we do not in fact know that those decisions exist? How can the Assembly establish that the president has violated the federal constitution, unless it actually has access to those decisions? If these decisions are not published, then the president of the republic is immune from any responsibility and innocent of any violation of the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, it's -- and it's not just the decisions, is it, because in Article 3 of Exhibit P2622, that's the 1992 rules of the Supreme Defence Council, it refers to: "Implementing the adopted decisions and conclusions." So the rules of the SDC seem to contemplate that conclusions are also going to be implemented; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rules from what year?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: 1992. I think that's tab -- I forgot. Tab 59. Sorry, Professor.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there you go. Article 8 of the rules, paragraph 2 reads: "The minutes comprise basic information on the work of a session, any decisions taken, or conclusions reached." It mentions decisions and conclusions. This certainly wasn't written down just like that. It must have a meaning. Article 3, paragraph 2: "The secretary of the Supreme Council helps the president prepare sessions and implement any decisions taken or conclusions reached." Therefore, the rules mention both decisions and conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I think you mentioned, last week, that these rules were never published, is that correct, the rules of procedure?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I never saw these rules published in the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at page 13049, you said: "Of course, if a regulation or rules have not been published, objectively they do not exist. They are not materialised in the legal world." But just because they don't exist in the legal world, Professor, what about the real world? I mean, even though the SDC apparently, according to the documents, never met after 23 March 1999, nor during the entire conflict, clearly the army was being commanded during that time. Wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I suggest to you that perhaps the president of the Republic of Yugoslavia, the supreme commander, Mr. Milosevic, didn't feel it was necessary to have the rules published, because as supreme commander he could tell General Ojdanic, the chief of the Supreme Command Staff, to do what needed to be done, and he could count on General Ojdanic and the army carrying it out, no?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the same applies to previous presidents of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, if you look at the office of the first president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Mr. Dobrica Cosic, when the first set of rules were adopted. If you look at the term of office of next president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Mr. Zoran Lilic, there were no rules of procedures published. And this sort of practice continued throughout the term of office of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Mr. Slobodan Milosevic, which started in July 1997 and went on to September 2000. This is a constant feature. For as long, you might say, as the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia existed, this continued, and you could say the same thing of the rules of procedure adopted during Mr. Vojislav Kostunica's time in office, that nothing was published.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, you mentioned, in connection with the SDC meetings, that you didn't see any instances of members of the SDC proposing amendments to the agenda. From your review of the documents, did you see that it appeared an agenda was circulated to the members sometime shortly prior to the meeting? Wasn't there usually some sort of notice that went out a day or two before the meeting listing the agenda items?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never actually saw a single invitation to a session; but whenever a session is scheduled, the invitation normally contains a proposed agenda. Whoever is being invited to a session, those are usually the members and officials being invited to attend a session of the Supreme Defence Council, probably receives a proposed agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's a good time for a break, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Professor, our break again for the morning, if you could please leave the courtroom with the usher. We shall resume again at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, at page 13061, on Tuesday last week, you were talking about the Supreme Defence Council, and you said: "It is not stated anywhere that the Supreme Defence Council is the highest organ of command and control of the Army of Yugoslavia." If it was not, then what body was, Professor, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certain based on what the constitution says is that the constitution does not define the Supreme Defence Council as the highest organ of command and control of the former Yugoslavia, such as the 1974 constitution, for example, which in Article 313 says explicitly that the Presidency of the SFRY is the highest organ of command and control of the Army of Yugoslavia, of the Army of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, in both peace and wartime. Based on this kind of wording, and especially in view of the constitutional powers, under Article 136 that he enjoys, it would seem to be the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. As I said a while ago, in most democratic constitutional systems across the world, the supreme commander of the army is the head of state; or, as we see in the case of Germany, for example, the prime minister, the chancellor, a civilian occupying this position, a state body must be appointed, the prime minister or the president of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. I think -- I see your point. But in Serbia and Yugoslavia at the time, the supreme commander of the army was the president of the Republic of Yugoslavia, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would seem to follow based on the article that we have read several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Although the constitution and the Law on Defence and the Law on the Army don't seem to contain the particular term "supreme commander," they make it clear that, in times of war and peace, the person who commands the army is the president of the republic, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've gone through all those articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And those all make it clear that he commands the army in peace and war, in accordance with decisions of the Supreme Defence Council, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in accordance with the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council, that's Article 135, paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it does not say in accordance with decisions of the General Staff of the VJ or the Supreme Command Staff of the VJ, but rather in accordance with the decisions of the SDC?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, at page 13065, Mr. Zecevic asked you if the Law on Defence was of a more general character than the Law on the Army, and you said: "Yes. It speaks of defence in general not a single subject of defence as the Law on the Army does." But between those two laws, the Law on Defence, which I think is P985, and the Law on the Army, which is P984, isn't the Law on Defence more specific and doesn't it have more details about the Supreme Defence Council, I think, in particular at Article 41?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You're right when you mention the Supreme Defence Council in this regard. This is Article 41. I thought it was another one, one coming before Article 41. That's what I thought a while ago. But this is a more general law, and you can tell that by looking at the number of articles that it contains, unlike the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia which is several times more comprehensive in terms of the number of its articles, more comprehensive, I'm saying, than the Law on Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, we've seen that the Supreme Defence Council apparently did not hold any meetings, or at least there's no record of meetings held, during the conflict after that 23rd of March, 1999 meeting; and, yet, the army obligation was being commanded and acting to carry out its constitutional obligation to defend the country. What is your explanation for how that took place if there were no meetings of the Supreme Defence Council? Do you have one?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regrettably, I'm unable to comment. I'm no military expert. I do know, however, of the conclusion that was adopted at the session of the Supreme Defence Council in October, saying that Yugoslavia was open, or rather, ready to tackle all open issues in a peaceful way. Should, however, the country be attacked, it would defend itself by all means. This was the basis for what was done between the sessions of the Supreme Defence Council, and we know that they weren't held for over a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have a moment to consult with my case manager.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, in connection with that, I propose to -- I want to read some answers or remarks from an interview that was conducted with General Pavkovic by the OTP concerning the SDC and a body that was referred to as the Supreme Command during the war and ask you to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see Mr. Aleksic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to raise an objection. My learned friend, Mr,. Hannis has not completed his question, nevertheless, I think that, during an exchange of positions under 98 bis, we discussed this. The Trial Chamber adopted certain guide-lines or even rulings for this interview that my client had with the OTP to be used against him alone and not against any of the other accused. So that is the gist of my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had discussed that on a couple of occasions, and we indicated that, yes, we intended it to be used only against General Pavkovic, except to the extent that it did not go to the acts and conduct of the other accused. And we argued at that time, Your Honour, that it was some evidence in which you could take into consideration about whether or not there was a body called the Supreme Command, whether it existed during a certain time-period. And also I note that General Pavkovic is listed as a witness who is going to testify later on in the case, in which case there would be an opportunity for the other five co-accused to cross-examine him. Professor Markovic is here now, and I would propose to ask him some questions about what General Pavkovic said in his interview about the existence of a body called the Supreme Command; otherwise, I would have to call him back later after General Pavkovic has testified. Now, if General Pavkovic doesn't testify and something I say during this colloquy with Professor Markovic touches on the acts and conduct of any of the accused other than General Pavkovic, I think Your Honours would be able to exclude that from your consideration of the evidence as to those other five later on in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall repel this objection and will allow the line of examination to continue. What Mr. Hannis appears to be seeking is evidence of this witness, not evidence of Pavkovic, in relation to matters on which General Pavkovic has made comments, and he's simply putting to this witness commenting for his reaction. We won't have a chance to get that at a later stage. If, of course, anything occurs here that might or could be seen to breach the guide-lines we previously discussed, then we are perfectly capable of distinguishing that from the rest of the material when we come to deliberate at the end of the case. So please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And for the benefit of my learned friends across the way, I intend to be reading from the interview which is Exhibit P949 at, I think, e-court pages 126 through 130. So they can follow along; and if there's a particular point, we can address it as we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, let me start. This is an interview of General Pavkovic by an investigator from the OTP, and they were talking about a body that we had seen referred to in some places as the Supreme Command. And the investigator, Kevin Curtis asked: "I know that you were only present twice, but did the Supreme Command meet in peacetime on a regular basis?" General Pavkovic's answer through the interpret was: "Supreme Command doesn't exist at the time of peace, that's the Supreme Defence Council at the time of peace. I don't know as to when they do meet; I think according to the needs." And Investigator Curtis asked: "Is the Supreme Defence Council and the Supreme Command, is it the same composition?" General Pavkovic's answer through the interpreter was: "No. The Supreme Defence Council is made of the president of the state of Yugoslavia and the presidents of the republican units," which we know and have talked about, "and that is the body from the time of peace. And the Supreme Command was formed by including the adequate or relevant military personnel who perform their duties. It has the supreme commander, also the head of the headquarters of the Supreme Command." Now, let me stop there for a moment, Professor. In that context, the supreme commander would be Mr. Milosevic, who we've referred to as being the one with the ultimate power to command the army, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you just -- do you mean the whole interview or just the last sentence when you are putting this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, the last -- my question was directed specifically at that last question about who the supreme commander would be that's being referred to there, and I take it that means Mr. Milosevic. Wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because at the time, he was the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And before I move on, did you want to comment on what I had read up to that point?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not really familiar with this topic. I would like to stick to the law and the constitution. The constitution says that the Army of Yugoslavia is commanded in peacetime and in wartime by the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in keeping with the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council in peacetime and in wartime. I do not know the military doctrine, and maybe these names of agencies are in keeping with the military doctrine. I don't know that, but I believe the constitutional provision is unequivocal and clear, and it is echoed in the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand your point, Professor. I'm not deliberately trying to put you in an uncomfortable position, but we -- we know that apparently the Supreme Defence Council, which is the body in accordance with whom -- whose decisions the president is to command the army in the time of peace and in the time of war, apparently did not meet during the war because there are no records of that, no documents to record that. The reason I'm asking you about this body that's referred to the Supreme Command is, I guess, to ask you if it is inconsistent with the constitution. Would it be unconstitutional for the Supreme Defence Council to basically remain in existence but expand to include some of these additional military personnel that General Pavkovic is describing in his interview. Given that from what we saw in other SDC meetings earlier, that sometimes additional individuals were invited to attend those meetings depending on the topics being considered. Is there anything to prevent the SDC expanding in that way?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The composition of the Supreme Defence Council is defined in Article 135, and it cannot be extended by any law. The SDC has three members and cannot have a single one more; however, other persons can be invited to attend sessions of the SDC. And we saw that on the 23rd of March, 1999, a decision of the SDC envisaged that the federal Minister for Defence and the Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia should attend. Perhaps other persons can be invited as well, depending on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And wouldn't you agree with me then on the 23rd of March, when you have an imminent threat of war, it made sense perhaps for the SDC to include the Chief of the General Staff of the army and the Minister of Defence if you are about to go into a war?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it would be logical. They could only contribute to increased competency of the discussion taking place at the council; plus, as far as I know, Yugoslavia did not want to engage in war. It had to because it was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the rule changes in the rules of procedure for the SDC on the 23rd of March, 1992 [sic], which called for the attendance of these additional personnel, did not change the way the SDC worked as far as who the deciding members were, did it? I mean, it's still President Milosevic and the presidents of the republics of Serbia and Montenegro who are the SDC who are going to take decisions and adopt conclusions, no?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Only the members of a body may take part in decision-making; non-members may not. They're only invited to attend sessions. They do not have the right of vote. They do not decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And I'll return to General Pavkovic's interview for a few more questions, and then he listed several different types of personnel that were included in this Supreme Command. He mentions, and this is on page 128: "There is a document which shows what the Supreme Command looked like and how it was composed." You haven't ever seen such a document, have you, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not, and I don't even know who is implied in the term "Supreme Command."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, we'll see what General Pavkovic had to say about that. He was asked next: "At what point does the Supreme Command come into effect?" He said: "The Supreme Command comes into effect when the state of war is declared." And then at the bottom of that page, Investigator Curtis asks: "So the president was involved with the Supreme Command and the presidents of the republic as well; is that correct?" General Pavkovic said: "Yes, Milutinovic and Djukanovic." Curtis asked: "Did they both participate actively in the Supreme Command?" Pavkovic says: "I saw Milutinovic but not Djukanovic." Curtis asks: "The only reason I ask is because in law can they function without the three of them being present." And General Pavkovic says: "Yes. It can function." And on the next page: "It has to function. The command system and the commanding of the units has to function, regardless of the fact whether the command is in the full composition or not." Would you agree with me that, during a state of war, the commanding body has to function. Whether or not there's a formal requirement for the SDC to have so many members present and these rules of procedure, wouldn't you agree with me, Professor, that as a practical matter during a state of war, whatever that body is and whoever the supreme commander is, it has to function in order for the army to do its job?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. The defence of the country is the supreme law. It's a maxim that applies to all countries and all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And a few lines on, General Pavkovic says: "I don't know what kind of flexibility I, as a commander, performed directives that I received from the Supreme Command." And that would be consistent with how the commanders in the army should work in conjunction with the supreme commander and any body in between, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to take this reservation once again. I'm not an expert in these issues, and I can only interpreted what the constitution and those two laws I mentioned say. This is not my field of expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand, Professor. Let's move on then to something else. I want to go now to your testimony from Wednesday, on the 8th of August, last week. There was a reference to the blue book, which is Exhibit 1D125, and you mentioned that this was an analysis of the constitutional position of the Republic of Serbia within the constitutional system after 1974. And you said this analysis was conducted by a Working Group. Who created this Working Group that put together the blue book?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the Working Group was set up by the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Serbia. It was a collective body that discharged the functions of the head of state.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this was a secret project, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The general public was not aware of the blue book. There were only rumours going around, and I had it for the first time in my hands and read it when I was about to testify in the Milosevic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know why it was a secret?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably because that blue book was a very well-substantiated critique of the constitution from 1974 and because many truths were stated in it that were unpleasant and embarrassing at the time to be stated in public. It was a time when the explanation of Edvard Kardelj applied unquestioningly. He was the leading constitutional expert, and the blue book questioned many of his ideas.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You'll have to help me out here, Professor. I'm not very familiar with this particular document. What in it was and what were the truths in it that were unpleasant and embarrassing. Unpleasant and embarrassing for whom?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were confusing and unpleasant, first of all, for the then-constitutional order; that is, the constitution of the SFRY and the constitution of the Republic of Serbia. That document showed that the provinces are becoming more and more distant from the republic that contained them, that they were becoming a state within the state, that they were not the same social and economic territory, that the constitution applied only to the territory between the two autonomous provinces, and that there was practically no republic power or government over the provinces, although they were formally, according to the constitution, part of the republic. The provinces were becoming a "corpus separatum," a separate body. They were rounding off their own statehood. They had constitutional, legislative, judicial, and constitutional judicial power, which brought into question the equality of the Republic of Serbia vis-a-vis other republics. And in light of the concept of the Yugoslav Federation, which is underlined by the self-determination of all peoples, the self-determination of the Serbian people was brought into question. Those were principles carved into the constitution of 1974, and those were the truths stated in that blue book, and they had to do -- they dealt with the constitutional position, the constitutional situation of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know when this Working Group was created?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was established a year after the adoption of the constitution, back in 1975, and it did its research, as we can read, in 1977, in March. And let me say that the blue book does not only analyse legal texts, it also analyses the practice, the constitutional practice, which often ran counter to the provisions of the constitution, all in the aim of emancipating and separating the provinces which were part of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When did this secret project or document cease to be a secret? When did it become public knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For all I know, it was published in 1990 in a publication, and it was accompanied by a brief foreword authored by a journalist for the Politika newspaper, Mr. Mirko Djekic, if I got the name right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was that after the changes to the constitution of Serbia had already been voted on in Vojvodina and Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One would have to know the month when the book was published, but the 1990 constitution of Serbia was adopted in September, the 28th September, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At page 13077 of your testimony last week, you were talking about the autonomous provinces under the 1974 constitution, and you say: "They enjoyed all the attributes of statehood, their constitutive executive and judicial authorities. They were self-sufficient entities." But the changes to the new constitution did take away those attributes of statehood from Vojvodina and Kosovo, did they not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. According to the constitution of 1990, they really acquired territorial autonomy within the Republic of Serbia instead of being rival states to Serbia, as the case had been in practice under the 1974 constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did they not have territorial autonomy before 1990?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the 1974 constitution, they had much more than that. They had all the attributes of statehood, which was unparalleled anywhere in the world. There was no state in the world with such a degree of decentralisation that they give constitution-making and judicial authority to their provinces. Constitution-making and the judiciary are attributes of statehood. If they had that, they should have been federal units; and under the 1974 constitution, they were not federal units.
