They had territorial autonomy within the Republic of Serbia, nominally, I'm saying, nominally; although, they had practically all the authorities of a state government.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mention that this was viewed as a threat to Serbia's right of self-determination, and you mentioned Serbia as -- the Serbian people being one of the constituent peoples of Yugoslavia. Who were the other constituent peoples of Yugoslavia at the time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Slovenes, Croats, Macedonians, Montenegrins, and there was Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was not an expression of the right of one people to self-determination. It was an atypical state unit because there were three peoples living in Bosnia-Herzegovina: Serbs, Croats, and Muslims, and none of them had absolute majority. That's why it was a historical acquisition. There was a reason in history why Bosnia and Herzegovina became a separate state unit, and the reason was that none of these peoples had absolute majority. In all the other federal units, the principle of self-determination applied for the appropriate constituent people. Macedonia, for instance, was the result of the Macedonian people's right to self-determination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You were discussing why it was viewed that Serbia needed to do something about this situation, where although it was one of the states that were a member of the greater Federation, they had a problem that they had two states within their state, referring to Kosovo and Metohija and Vojvodina. And you said the problem, at page 13077, the problem was that: "This resulted in a splintering of Serbia's economy and jeopardized their internal domestic market." Could you explain to us how this was, the existence of Kosovo and Vojvodina cause a splintering of the economy? I'm no economist, so I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only of the economy, but of the legal system as well. That means that the economic and legal territory was being rounded off, and those areas were becoming self-sufficient as an economic and legal entity. As far as the legal system is concerned, there was almost complete parallelism between the laws that applied in the Republic of Serbia and the laws that applied in the provinces. Every regulation adopted by the republic would be adopted by the respective province. They were building themselves as self-sufficient units, which was probably one way to eventually perform the secession, especially in the case of Kosovo, as was the case after all with republics later. The republics left Yugoslavia, as already-established, fully established, economic entities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You were asked by Mr. Zecevic, at page 13078, why these autonomous provinces were set up within the Republic of Serbia. You mentioned three reasons: First was historical background, second was ethnic context, and the third would be the peculiarity of these areas in terms of their economies in relation to Serbia as a whole. Could you elaborate on that a little bit. What was the historical background regarding setting up Kosovo and Vojvodina as autonomous provinces within the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the historical context was provided by the historical facts. Kosovo and Metohija, after the liberation of Serbia from Turkish occupation, which had lasted for several centuries, and this liberation, or rather, Serbia was granted independence in 1878 at the Berlin Congress. And Kosovo and Metohija, as part of the territory of the Serbian medieval state, was restored once it was liberated from Turkish occupation only in the Balkan wars in 1912. So it was only in 1912 that this territory was joined to the then-kingdom of Serbia, but that territory had belonged to Serbia all along, only it had been under Turkish occupation, as all of Serbia was once. As regards Vojvodina, after the end of World War I in 1918, when the Austro-Hungarian empire fell apart of which it had been a part, its Assembly adopted a decision on joining the kingdom of Serbia. So in 1918, on the 1st of December, the common state was created of the kingdom of Serbia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, I'm going to interrupt you there. Mr. Hannis, is this the sort of material you wish to support your case, because this answer is going to last until lunchtime --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- unless you concentrate the questions on things that are important to the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I think for my purposes I can move on. Let me move then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I remained interested in the concept of the splintering of the economy which I could not understand, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, that is the third reason that you gave, Professor, was the peculiarity of these areas in terms of their economies and their peculiarity in relation to the Republic of Serbia. Could you answer that one for us.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first reason was historical. It's a historical specificity. Secondly was its specific ethnic make-up, because it's an area inhabited by numerous ethnic minorities. One predominates in Kosovo and Metohija; whereas, a multitude of ethnic groups are present in Vojvodina. And then, thirdly, it's the geographic specificity of these areas. The fragmentation of the economy was due to the fact that plants were duplicated, for example, so that the territory of each province would become economically self-sufficient. That's the way in which the unified legal and economic territory of the republic was being fragmented. The provinces were setting themselves up as independent wholes, independent of the Republic of Serbia. For this reason, there was duplication of commercial and production facilities. The rights and the competencies of the Republic of Serbia ended at the borders of the autonomous provinces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Which rights and competencies of Serbia ended at the borders of the autonomous provinces?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the rights of every state anywhere. They stopped at the borders of the provinces, the competencies of the state. Starting from the border of the autonomous province you would have another legal system. It would be the provincial laws that were in force, the jurisdiction of the provincial courts. There would be a separate constitution protected by the provisional Constitutional Court, so everything that characterises an independent state. That's the way in which the idea of an autonomous province from the 1974 constitution was being abused. Via facti, they were transforming themselves into federal units, or rather, into independent states. And we have already seen that four federal units when -- once they had set themselves up as self-sufficient wholes seceded from the Yugoslav Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about internal security? Serbia had a Ministry of Interior. Who -- did Vojvodina and Kosovo have their own separate Ministries of Interior?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They had their provincial Ministries of the Interior. They weren't called ministries at the time. They were called secretariats, because in the 1974 constitution the principle was unity of power rather than division of power. There were executive councils and secretariats instead of ministries, and this was in the spirit of the Assembly system. It was a quite different constitutional order from the one established in the constitution of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the relationship between the Secretariat of Interior in Kosovo or Vojvodina with the Ministry of Interior in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the 1974 constitution was in force, every organ was the highest organ on its territory within the sphere of its competence. So it was an autonomous organisation. The entire state organisation, the organisation of the state administration, did not have a hierarchical structure except to the extent envisaged in Article 301 of the constitution of the Republic of Serbia of 1974 where this was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So did the Ministry of Interior of Serbia and policemen who worked for them between 1974 and 1989, did they have no authority within Kosovo or Vojvodina? Is that what you're telling me?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did have authority when republican laws had to be enforced on the entire territory of the Republic of Serbia, and these laws are taxatively enumerated in the 1974 constitution of the Republic of Serbia. This was not a large number of laws, because for the most part legislative power was vested in the autonomous provinces. The republican laws, as a rule, applied on the territory outside the autonomous provinces on the territory of Republic of Serbia where no constitution -- where no autonomous provinces had been constituted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, Professor. Thank you. You were talking about -- we've been talking about the blue book and the reason that that project was started. It seemed that it was concerned with the representation of the autonomous provinces in the Federation, that they were basically rising to the level being almost equal to Serbia, the state of which -- the republic of which they were a part. Was there any attempt to solve this problem by amending the constitution of Yugoslavia, the federal constitution, instead of trying to do it by amending the constitution of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was never amended by the federal constitution, nor could the constitution of the republic alter the position of the provinces in the federal constitution. So even after the amendments to the Serbian constitution, the provinces continued to have the same status in the federal constitution. They simply did not have the same competencies within Serbia that they had had under the 1974 Serbian constitution. So the constitution of the Republic of Serbia did not impinge on the status of the autonomous provinces within the Federation. They were still represented in all federal organs, in the Assembly of the SFRY, in the council of republics and autonomous provinces. They had an eight-member delegation. They were represented in the Presidency of the SFRY with one member, just like every republic was. And in the Constitutional Court they also had one member each; whereas, the republics had two, and in the federal court likewise. So nothing there was changed by the 1990 Serbian constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With regard to the blue book, you referred to it in your testimony at page 13084 as "an official document." What do you mean by "official document"? Of what entity or government was it an official document?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a document established by the body of a state organ, so it was not done by a group of expert authors on their own initiative, rather, a state organ, the Presidency of the SFRY, set up a Working Group. I have explained what the composition of the group was, and that Working Group after dealing with the task entrusted to it systematically produced the blue book. In that sense, it was an official document. It was not a private project embarked on by the authors of the book. They didn't get together spontaneously on their own initiative. It was a task entrusted to that body by a state organ, the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I didn't see on the document when I looked at it. Is there any official seal or stamp or signature on that copy of the blue book that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have it here in The Hague, but believe me I didn't look at that. I was dealing with the contents, not the external appearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Zecevic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If the authenticity of the document is in question, we can provide the original of the blue book to my learned colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That was my understanding. I'm sorry, maybe I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm satisfied with that. I can deal with Mr. Zecevic on that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, there was one item in the transcript from this day that I needed to ask you about. I think maybe there was a mistake. At page 13091, you were speaking of amendments to the Serbian constitution, and they refer to the amendments to the constitution we mentioned a bit earlier, the 1989 amendments. They were passed by the Assembly of the SFRY and the Assemblies of the two autonomous provinces. Is that correct? Is it the Assembly of the SFRY or the Assembly of Serbia or both?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it says the Assembly of the SFRY, it's an error. It should say the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia and both autonomous provinces. They gave their agreement to the amendments to the constitution of the Republic of Serbia which were enacted in 1989. You know, the names were often changed. The word "socialist" was put in and then thrown out, so one can easily make this slip when speaking because of these frequent changes of name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. No problem, Professor. I make it many times. At page 13091, a little further down, you were saying that this decision, or the passing of these amendments, the Assembly made a finding or stated that it believed that these changes, these amendments to the constitution of Serbia do not affect, do not change, in any way the position of the socialist autonomous provinces established by the constitution. Sir, it seemed to me that before these changes, Kosovo and Vojvodina had a Constitutional Court, had a constitution, had the right basically to veto changes to the higher constitution. How can you say that these changes, these amendments did not affect, did not change in any way their position?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This goes for the changes in the constitution of the Republic of Serbia carried out by the amendments of 1989. The constitution itself was from 1974. The Assembly of the SFRY says that these changes do not alter the constitutionally established status of the autonomous provinces in the Federation, and that's true. The Assembly of the SFRY stated this at the joint session, where all the republics and both autonomous provinces were represented. Under the 1990 constitution, the status of the provinces changed completely. They no longer had constitutional power, their own courts, and so on. They had all this based on the 1989 amendments.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But it certainly changed, if I understand your answer correctly, you say it didn't change their position with regard to the federal constitution and their position with regard to the Federation of Yugoslavia. But it certainly did change the position of the autonomous provinces vis-a-vis their relationship with the Republic of Serbia, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the Republic of Serbia was sovereign, so it could amend its constitution, of course, within the limits set by the federal constitution. So it had the power to amend its own constitution. This amendment could not be contrary to the federal constitution; but in everything else, the Republic of Serbia was free to order relations on its own territory through its own constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At page 13092, I guess I wasn't paying enough attention, and I think I let my colleague Mr. Zecevic get away with a bit of a leading question. He asked you at line 6: "That means that neither Kosovo nor Vojvodina were stripped of autonomy, but rather that a redistribution of competencies was done between the organs of autonomous provinces and the Republic of Serbia, correct?" And you said: "Yes." Now, in connection with the "redistribution of competencies," isn't it true that all the redistribution that was going on was one-way, wasn't it, from the provinces, from Vojvodina and Kosovo, to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. It was one-way, precisely because the powers of the autonomous provinces had been exaggerated. The autonomous provinces had had a lot more than this form of territorial decentralisation implies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Professor, I remind you of a comment from Judge Bonomy earlier in your testimony about: "You can't change the nature of a dog by calling it a cat." This phrase "redistribution of competencies," isn't it fair to say that what from Serbia looked like redistribution of competencies might in Kosovo look like revocation of autonomy?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why was it not understood as revocation of autonomy in Vojvodina then? It was not revocation of autonomy. It was simply reducing the autonomy to the normal limits of this form of territorial decentralisation. Any state is authorised to do this. It falls within the scope of state sovereignty. That's what state sovereignty implies. What kind of order a state will prescribe in its own constitution is up to the state. That's what the sovereignty of constitutional power consists in. It can -- may or may not introduce decentralisation, a parliamentary or a central system of government. It can have a Constitutional Court, but it needn't have one. It can be the regularly courts that monitor implementation of the constitution. All of this falls within the scope of sovereign state power. There's no regulation that would make it binding on a state to introduce territorial autonomy so great that it would be tantamount to the independence of the units concerned. No one can impose that on a state, including the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, Professor. Let's move to another topic. At page 13093, Mr. Zecevic was asking you about citizenship, and Article 47 deals with citizenship of the Republic of Serbia. It says: "A citizen of the Republic of Serbia may not be deprived of his citizenship, exiled, or extradited." What about being deported or forcibly displaced within the republic? Article 47 doesn't deal with those situations, does it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Deportation has to do with the constitutional freedom to reside in a certain place and freedom of movement. So freedom of movement and habitation is not absolute. It can be limited in four cases, the four cases envisaged in the constitution: One of them when this is required for the defence of the country, then it's to prevent the spread of contagious diseases. Another reason is criminal proceedings being instituted, and so on. We can find those provisions and read them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Related to that Mr. Zecevic asked you a hypothetical question about a Yugoslav citizen leaving the territory, losing their identity papers or their passport or their passport seized, and he said: "They don't lose their Yugoslav citizenship just because something like that happens, right?" And your answer was: "No, they do not use their citizenship. The same thing applies to an ordinary citizen who simply loses his ID. He simply gets a new one. That's all there is to it." Let me give you a hypothetical that's more related to some of the evidence in our case. Say a family is routed by police and soldiers early in the morning from their home. All the men are shot. The women and children are told to go to Albania, that Serbia is not theirs. On the way or at the border, they're forced to surrender their ID documents, which they see torn up or burned. And in real life, how does that work? Technically, I take it your position is they haven't lost their citizenship, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But in real life, how is that going to work? You know we talked about 16 decrees that were issued during the state of war, and one of them was the Law on ID Cards, which provided, as I recall, that if a person came to be without their identity card, what they were supposed to do is report it to the Ministry of Interior in the municipality where they came to be without their card within a certain brief amount of time; and then within, I think, something like eight days, they were supposed to go to their home municipality and request a new one. In the circumstances that I described, how are they going to be able to do that? If the card is taken from them at the border by the police, is it likely that in real life they're going to report to the local police about that seizure of their identity card?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this is getting into speculation, and it's just extending this beyond any relevance to proper questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The practical impact of this law is an important issue in the case if it had one; and if the witness can assist us by dealing with this hypothetical question, then he should do so. We do not consider that the question goes outwith the realms of relevance in this case, and therefore we will repel the objection and allow the question to be answered. Can you help us, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't have the relevant laws before me, but it's quite clear that this would apply to a citizen of the Republic of Serbia who is on Serbian territory and has no ID on him. The deadlines are somewhat shorter than those that apply to the Law on Identity Cards, and that is not the law in the 1974 tab. The law was adopted later, and it was adopted in line with the 1990 constitution. So that's the answer. This applies to citizens of the Republic of Serbia who are on Serbian territory. The republic must know who exactly is on its territory. On their return to the country, what applies is not the same law that applies in a state of war, or rather, the decree that applies in a state of war, but the Law on Identity Cards that applies in normal, regular, peacetime circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I guess the point I was trying to make, Professor, was that although technically those circumstances, as I describe, might not amount to a legal loss of citizenship; as a de facto matter, it is the equivalent of losing your citizenship under those circumstances, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand why that would de facto be the case. Legally, this person is still a citizen. What happened is this person lost his documents. They no longer have an ID or a passport, but that does not affect his status as a citizen. He remains a citizen. The only thing he doesn't have to show for it is a document, but he will get one issued sooner or later. As far as ID, passport, or any other public document is concerned, if you lose one of these or mislay one of these, this has no legal consequences in terms of your citizenship. It doesn't legally affect your citizenship.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me move on to page 13106. You were talking about the law that was enacted by the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Serbia to -- with a view to implementing the provisions of the constitution in 1974. I think this is tab 77 in your grey binder. It's Exhibit 1D458, the Law on Temporary Measures for Social Protection of Self-management Rights, et cetera. How were these -- how were these triggered, Professor? What was happening in October 1989 to bring this about?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what exactly you would say to bring this about. These provisional measures were applied alike throughout Yugoslavia. These are provisional measures for the social protection of self-management right and socially owned property or part of the federal unit of the Federation. These weren't only applied in Kosovo and Metohija. There are numerous cases where these were applied to Serbia proper, as well as in other republics. The federal facilities were also protected by the self-management rights; therefore, this is a provision contained in the federal constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you, there has been evidence in this case about "special measures" is the term that I've heard used most often, I think, being applied in Kosovo in 1989/1990. Do you know what I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Special" and "provisional" are not exactly synonymous. Provisional measures for the social protection of self-management rights and socially owned property. There are reasons specified here as to when these measures are to be taken and by who. They're not for the Republic of Serbia to take, but rather organs, a Municipal Assembly or a provisional Assembly, depending on the measure itself, or perhaps the ombudsman in case of local self-government. When Serbia's constitution is changed or amended and an entirely new social system was introduced, the need for this law ceased, because self-management and socially owned property were no longer notions present in the 1990 constitution, and they no longer remained constitutional elements under the 1990 constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was there some similar provision that was implemented to take their place in light of the changed circumstances?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in that constitution, nor were there any such laws which, therefore, would have been without a constitutional basis. These laws, one by one, ceased to apply following the adoption of the 1990 constitution by the Republic of Serbia, simple reason being these were a reflection of the old constitutional order which was now superseded by the new one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there not a finding by the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia that the conditions in Kosovo were such that special measures needed to be applied throughout the entire province of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me see which law I have in front of me. All right. This is the Republic of Serbia. Provisional measures are to be taken by the Municipal Assembly that wherever the headquarters of the self-managing organisation happens to be, and the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia takes measures against any organisation which it established, where the republican organs are in charge of monitoring the legality of operations. That's what Article 9 on the Law on Self-management, et cetera, seems to suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me go to another matter for the moment. At page 13119, Mr. Zecevic was asking you about the Ministry of Defence, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the Ministry of Economic Relations with Foreign Countries which had been envisioned in the new constitution of 1990, even though these were matters within the competences of the still-existing Federation. And he showed you an exhibit. I think it was tab 18. 1D142 is the exhibit number, and there was a law which abolished these ministries or decree that they would cease to exist then. That was 30th of August, 1993. Do you find that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, do you know why it took so long to do away with those ministries that weren't necessary?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was necessary for the same reasons as it was to adopt the 1990 constitution of the Republic of Serbia. The Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia still exists; whereas, the republics that were about to secede are doing everything to achieve this secession. Given what conditions prevailed, this was a tool of defence and that is the purpose of the 1990 constitution. In case a total secession and of the break-up of Yugoslavia, Serbia now has a defence ministry and a foreign office. When the 1992 constitution of the Republic of Serbia was adopted, under which Serbia and Montenegro organised themselves into a new Federation, "the rump Yugoslavia," as it was termed at the time, the Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, the need ceased to exist for those ministries to still be around, simply because those ministries were in charge of duties and tasks that now fell under the jurisdiction of the Federation under Article 78 of the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia 1992 constitution. What is noteworthy is that Montenegro kept those ministries throughout. They did not abolish those ministries. For as long as Montenegro existed as part of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, they kept a Foreign Office, a Ministry of the Interiors, and I think also a Foreign Defence Ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think it's time for the lunch break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Time for lunch now, Professor. We'll break now and we will resume at 1.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.45 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It came to me at the end of the last session that the topic I was trying to get to involved two exhibits, which I had not previously indicated to the Defence I was going to show this witness. They are exhibits already in evidence in the Prosecution's case, Exhibit P1854 and P1855, and I've asked Mr. Zecevic if he had any objection to my showing that to Professor Markovic at this time. I understand he does not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, I'd like to show you Exhibit 1 -- Exhibit P1854. It's my understanding that this was published in the Official Gazette of Serbia on the 26th of June, 1990, entitled "The Law on the Action of Republican Agencies Under Special Circumstances." Have you seen that before? Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And related to that is Exhibit P1855, also dated the 26th of June, 1990, and that's a decision establishing that special circumstances have arisen in the territory of the socialist autonomous province of Kosovo. Have you seen that before or were you aware of that decision?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was all before the entry into force of the 1990 Serbian constitution. It was while the 1974 constitution was in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you -- were you aware of any debate that went on in connection with the passage of this law in June of 1990?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of the law; however, at that time, I was only a university professor. I did not hold any public office, so I am not very familiar with the history and the background of that law. All I know is that such a law exists, and there is a decision passed on the basis of that law, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on the 26th of June, 1990, was the new constitution of Serbia in effect yet?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The new constitution of the Republic of Serbia was passed on the 28th September 1990, and this one, as far as I can see, was the 26th of June, 1990. So the old constitution of the Republic of Serbia was still in place then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But by the 26th of June, 1990, the autonomous province of Kosovo had already had their vote regarding the proposed amendments to the constitution. That was done in March of 1989, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The vote was to pass amendments to the constitution of March 1989, not to adopt a new constitution, so it was about amendments to the constitution of the 1974 constitution of Serbia. They were adopted in March 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Constitutionally speaking, under what provision would this kind of law come as far as the powers of the republic Assembly? In essence, it seems like sort of a republic level state of emergency.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the law before me to check its contents. It certainly invokes some constitutional grounds for adopting -- what I'm trying to say is I can't remember the contents of that law precisely because it was enacted 17 years ago. In order to speak about it, I would have to have it before me. But I know that such a law existed, and it became null and void when the 1990 constitution was passed. There is a whole list of laws that ceased to be in force with the passing of that constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask if the registry officer could put up Exhibit P1854.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I'll have you look at that, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This is -- maybe I've got my numbers crossed. I think this is 1855 on the screen now, and I'm looking for 1854. And I think we have to go to page 2 of the English version because it was a two-sided book that was copied with B/C/S on one side and English on the other. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't know, Professor, if you can see Article 2 under the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We may have to scroll down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This Article 2 seems to describe under what circumstances -- special circumstances shall be deemed to have arisen. Do you see that? It includes activities directed overseeing the constitutional order, failure to comply with laws, acts which may be hazardous for human life and health.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that; and after the reference to these grounds, it says: "The Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Serbia shall determine at the proposal of the Executive Council," and now we need to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You need now to go to the top of the next column to see the rest of that sentence? My question was, Professor: In general, this seems to be some sort of republic level state of emergency; is that a fair analogy?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the law does not say explicitly "state of emergency." It says: "Measures to be taken under special circumstances."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But would you agree with me that the special circumstances described in Article 2 are somewhat similar to those that the Federal Assembly of Yugoslavia would consider in deciding whether a state of emergency existed or not? I mean, it seems to provide for natural disasters as well as activities aimed at overthrowing the constitutional order. In general, it seems similar, does it not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. The grounds are similar as those invoked with regard to the state of emergency.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Constitutionally speaking, is this -- is this a competency that is reserved for the federal government only or is this something that the republic can do as well without intruding on the competencies of the federal body, the Federation?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I would need to have for me the constitution of the Republic of Serbia, the one that was passed 33 years ago, in order to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. It's not important for me at this point. A related question I have, though, is: That law is published on the 26th of June --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Zecevic on his feet. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just one clarification. I believe the professor meant the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Serbia. I mean, just to have a distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed. Thank you. The 33 years ago is consistent with that. Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The law itself seems to have been passed on the 26th, and then the decision establishing that special circumstances, indeed, having arisen in Kosovo, is passed the same day. Does that strike you as unusual?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But one should look at the final provision of this law, stating when it enters into force. If it enters into force on the date of its publication, then it's perfectly all right. If there is no normal "vacatio legis," that is, the eight-day delay from adoption to publication, we should look at the final provision of this law, stating when it enters into force.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, certainly, the decision that special circumstances have arisen makes reference to the law on the procedure to be followed. And if this decision is to take effect on the date it's published, which appears to be the 26th of June, the same date as the decision itself, that would seem to indicate that the law on the procedure must have been effective on or before the 26th of June, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way it should be chronologically, but I repeat, we should look at the last article of the law to be quite sure, to avoid all speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, I think we're going to have to do that later because from what I see on my copy of the law this is published in a book and it's not the Official Gazette version, and I don't see the last page with the date on it. I'll work with Mr. Zecevic on trying to get a copy of the Official Gazette to substitute in its place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not possible that if we go to the last page of this version that we will actually get it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's worth a look, Your Honour, but I printed out a hard copy and the last page of my hard copy doesn't contain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's on the last page, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It does, Your Honour, Article 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, could you read Article 20 to us, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 20 reads: "This law shall enter into force on the day of its promulgation in the Official Gazette of the Socialist Republic of Serbia." That's what I assumed. It entered into force on the day of its publication.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And is there anything unusual about a decision, taken in light of this newly passed law on the 26th of June, 1990, taking place on the same day? Would there normally be some waiting period or some transition period?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, there should be a delay. It's called "vacatio legis," a delay between the enactment and publication; but, in this case, the law enters into force on the day of its publication. If it was published on the 26th of June, then it's not against the law to enforce it after that date because it already is in force then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Professor. I'll move on to another topic. At page 13113, from your testimony on last Wednesday, Mr. Zecevic was talking to you about Exhibit P1857, dated the 5th of July, 1990. And you pointed out, in connection with that, pursuant to the 1990 constitution, the provinces no longer had legislative power. They were able to issue decisions -- their Assemblies were able to issue decisions, but no longer legislation. They also no longer could adopt statutes as the highest legislative enactments. Can you tell me, what is a legislative decision and how does it differ from legislation?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The decision is like a bylaw. Its legal force is less than a law. That's what a decision is. But provinces lost legislative power while keeping the power of enforcement, but their laws had to be in accordance with the laws of the republic. This is dealt with in Article 109, paragraph 1, item 3 of the constitution of the Republic of Serbia. It says that: "Autonomous provinces shall adopt general enactments, in keeping with the constitution and the law, to regulate certain issues that are of interest that are pertinent to the citizens in various fields, various areas," and those areas are listed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. As a matter of fact, in, I think, July 1990, didn't the Serbian Assembly, the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia, disband or suspend the Assembly of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That would be the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That was the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Serbia, and it did so through a special law. It was all before the adoption of the constitution of the Republic of Serbia of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Professor, I think you'll be happy to hear I'm going to try and direct my next series of questions more to your evidence of fact rather than your expert report. I want to go to March of 1998. At page 13124, you told us that in early 1998, in March, the prime minister gave you the responsibility of involving yourself in talks with the leaders of Albanian parties. Who was the prime minister in March of 1998?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In March 1998, the prime minister was late Mirko Marjanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at the time he contacted you about this, did he explain why -- well, I can understand why he picked you for the job, but did he explain why this was being done at this particular time? And I think we established the date was around the 11th of March, 1998.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time, there were demands of the international community in this sense. Later came the resolution of the UN Security Council demanding this kind of contact, and simultaneously the activities of the KLA escalated. So the time seemed right to try a new tack, a peaceful political dialogue, to try to resolve the conflict in Kosovo and Metohija that had given rise to armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, were you aware that on, I think, the 5th of March, 1998, there was a MUP anti-terrorist operation involving a man named Adem Jashari, and there was a rather highly publicised incident in which a number of women and children, in addition to some of the suspected terrorists, were killed? Were you aware of that at the time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about that from reading newspapers. Kosovo and Metohija was not in my line of work and, as I said, I first began to deal with issues of Kosovo and Metohija, and then only at the negotiating level, after the 10th of March, 1998. My job was to negotiate and to frame the results of those negotiations in the form of some enactments that all the participants would agree on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When the prime minister asked you to participate in this, did he -- did he advise you about whether or not there had been any ongoing efforts by other individuals or groups to negotiate with the Albanian parties and their leaders?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't tell me that. And as far as I know, that was the first organised effort by the government to conduct these negotiations. From the ranks of its own members, the cabinet chose this four-member delegation while addressing an appeal to all the parliamentary parties, all their clubs, to join in the delegation in order to preserve the unity of the position among parliamentary parties on all the issues involved in the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you personally, Professor, ever have any discussions with Mr. Milosevic about negotiations with the Kosovo Albanians?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't, for the simple reason, because as you have seen yourself, the negotiations didn't happen. The Albanians did not respond to any of our numerous appeals, so I had nothing to report on, to him or to Mr. Marijanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did anyone ever inform you or advise you or suggest to you that there may have been other efforts at negotiating, perhaps more informal or secret negotiations, with some of the Kosovo Albanian leaders?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never informed of anything like that. To the best of my knowledge, as I was in the government at the time, this was the first time that the government was embarking on such negotiations in an organised way. Whether there had been any informal talks on an individual basis, I don't know, but I believe there were none under the auspices of the government. This was the first time that, under the auspices of the government, a delegation known to the public was going to Pristina to negotiate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you say "a government" in that context, you're referring to the Government of the Republic of Serbia, correct, not Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. All the time I've been referring to the Government of the Republic of Serbia, of which I was a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct. Thank you. You were asked, I think, at page 13127, about Mr. Tanic, Ratomir Tanic. And in connection with negotiations, you said he was never given any tasks by the government, he was not a public official, and that you met him physically only once "when the German Ambassador Mr. Gruber invited us to lunch." First of all, when was that that Ambassador Gruber invited you to lunch?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't recall the date, believe me, but it's well-known in what period he was the ambassador to the then-Yugoslavia, Mr. Gruber I mean. But believe me, I can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ambassador of Great Britain attended that lunch as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can't remember it right now. It escapes me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I can't either. You said he "invited us to lunch." Who was "us," you and who else?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Gruber invited me, and the reason was for him to hand over to me a book on the autonomy of southern -- of the southern Tyrol. I didn't know anybody else was going to attend the lunch. It was a very relaxed, informal lunch. Many issues were discussed. Probably the situation on Kosovo and Metohija was among the topics of discussion, but there were many, many topics that were talked about, and I remember having seen Mr. Tanic on that occasion. Up to that point, I had seen him only on television. I'm absolutely certain that that was the first and the last time I ever saw him in person. Mr. Tanic was in no way connected to the Government of the Republic of Serbia. I don't know in what capacity he came or could have come into contact with the Government of the Republic of Serbia. His party was in opposition at the time, or his parties, rather, in the plural, because he switched parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you know him at one time to be associated or affiliated or a member of the party New Democracy?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After the Civil Alliance, a political party of which he was a prominent member, he became a member of New Democracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as I understand Dusan Mihajlovic was part of that party.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. He was the leader, so to speak, of that political party?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This luncheon, I know you say you don't recall the date, but was the date sometime after March 11th of 1998, once you had been assigned the responsibility of trying to associate with the Kosovo Albanians? Was it sometime after that date and sometime before the war in March of 1999, if we can narrow it down to a year anyway?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was certainly not after March 1998, but one could see when Mr. Gruber was the ambassador to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And how big a group was this at lunch? You mentioned yourself, the British ambassador, Mr. Gruber, Mr. Tanic, that's four of you. Was this a group of 50 or a hundred or just the four of you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, just the four of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, excuse me. Now I remember. There was also Mr. Branko Brankovic, who at the time was an official in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. That's right. I'm sure he was at that lunch as well, Mr. Branko Brankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Professor. Then you mention -- you start to tell us about your efforts to actually sit down and talk with the Kosovo Albanians, and initially -- initially, there was a meeting scheduled. There was a public announcement scheduled and invitations sent out to private addressees, and you think the first meeting was supposed to be on the 12th of March. So how far in advance of the meeting was this public announcement made? If you only got assigned the task on the 10th or the 11th, it couldn't have been too far in advance, could it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It couldn't have been too far in advance, but I think it can be seen from that public communique. I'm sure there must be a date on it. I don't know whether it was issued on the 10th. I think it was, because that was when the government had -- or rather, the cabinet held a session, and, usually, a communique would be issued right after each session. So it should have been issued on the same day, the 10th of March, but I'm sure there must be a date on it anyway, on the communique, to show when it was published.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we can have a look for that. I want to read you about a couple of documents that came out during the time between the Jashari incident that I asked you about on the 5th of March, 1998, and the 12th of March that we've been about the scheduled meeting. We can show these to you, but I don't think you'll need to read them for the purposes of my question. 1D551 is a statement of the MUP of the 5th of March, 1998, which talked about the killing of "hard-core terrorists" in connection with that Jashari operation, and there was no mention of civilians in that first statement. 1D552 was another statement of the MUP on the 6th of March, again no mention of killing of civilians. It was only on the 11th of March, that is, one day before your scheduled meeting, that 1D553, another MUP statement, a preliminary report, came out and indicated that civilians had been killed in that operation. So I guess my question is to you is: Is it surprising that given that circumstances that were going on at that time, that there might have been a certain amount of fear and mistrust on the part of Kosovo Albanian in negotiating with Serb authorities? You know that was a highly publicised incident and large outcry about that in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards security, I don't think that can be a reason because the talks were scheduled by the Government of the Republic of Serbia, which guaranteed the security of both sides participating in the talks. I do allow that it might have been an expression of dissatisfaction or outrage, but certainly security or a threat to the security of members of the Albanian delegation did not exist. The security put in place was very strong, both as regards the building where the talks were to take place and the approaches to that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, Professor. We've heard that the notice about the meeting may not have gone out very far in advance. Do you know how far in advance the personal invitations went out on that occasion for the 12th of March meeting? Did you issue those or were they issued by somebody else?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I signed them. How they were sent out, technically, I don't know. Let's say they could not receive them, did not receive them, for that week, but they would certainly have received them for the following week because there was an intervening weekend. And with respect to the meeting scheduled in the following week, they would certainly have been able to respond and I'm sure they received the invitations. You see, Mr. Fehmi Agani said that he had received my invitation in one of the documents we read out here all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Professor, we'll take a look at that in a little bit. With regard to your efforts at negotiating with some of the Albanian leaders, did you ever hear of a group called "G-15" or a smaller group called "G-5," referring to certain Kosovo Albanian leaders?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if I told you that among that G-5 group, one of those members was Veton Surroi and another was Mr. Rugova, and that they had a meeting with Mr. Milosevic, I think, in May of 1998, were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what "G-5" refers to. As far as I can recall, I did not attend any such meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, so when you went down on the 12th of March, nobody showed up for that first meeting, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you were aware at that time in March of 1998 that the international community seemed to be keeping an eye on and showing some concern about events in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was aware of that at the time, and a resolution of the Security Council has been shown here concerning this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's right. We'll talk about that, too, in a few minutes. So after you went on the 12th and nobody was there, I think you testified, at page 13130 and 131, that you went again the next day, on the 13th. I think you told us that was Thursday and Friday of that week in 1998, and then the following week you went on every working day and scheduled a meeting in the same place at the same time every day and informed the leaders of the Albanian parties. Did you send them an invitation every day for the following day or how did that work?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The invitations were sent out every day for the following day, and a new meeting was scheduled on every following day. And they should have known that a meeting had been scheduled at a certain time and in a certain place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How many days did you continue to do that for? You told us about the 12th and 13th and then the following week beginning Monday, the 16th. Did you do it every day that week?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of that week, we did it every day, all the five working days of that week.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Still no meeting, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Still no meeting, but now the representatives of those two Albanian political parties which were not majority parties responded. I've told you their names, Mr. Faik Jashari and Mr. Sokol Qausha, as did the representatives of the other ethnic communities in Kosovo and Metohija who said that they, too, were citizens of Kosovo and Metohija, and that one could not talk about the status of Kosovo and Metohija only in negotiations between the Albanians and the Serbs. They wanted to be included, too; the Turks, the Goranci, the Roma, the Egyptians, the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know what party Mr. Faik Jashari represented?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it written down. It's in my bag. I think it was the Party for Democratic Initiative, something like that. The names of these parties were all very similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you have any idea at the time or do you know now how big a party that was, what its constituency was?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were small political parties. The fact that they recognised that Kosovo was part of the Republic of Serbia and that the status of Kosovo had to be solved as part of the Republic of Serbia, the fact that this was the ideology and platform of these parties shows that they could only have a small following. It was mostly the parties who were in favour of the independence of Kosovo and Metohija who had the largest following.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. You told us that there were no state organs involved in your negotiation. What do you mean by state organs? Do you mean ministries or what in that context?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from the cabinet, and later on the envoy of the president of the republic, or rather, the government delegation and later on the envoy of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, representative of an other state organ participated in those talks, the talks with the representatives of those ethnic communities who responded to the invitations. Later on we saw that President Milutinovic also joined in those talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we look next at Exhibit P445.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Professor, I think this is tab number 9, I think, in your red binder. I don't know if you have the red ones with you today or not.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it. That's Resolution 1160 of the Security Council of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this is --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that tab 9?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's what I had in the transcript; is that correct? Tab 9? Yes. It is the UN resolution from March of 1998. And you testified at page 13142 that -- that everything that this resolution mentioned is something that the Government of Serbia had already done. And what is also important for me, looking at this resolution, is the qualification given in the preamble where they say -- where it says that they condemn all terrorist operations on the part of the KLA. Do you see that provision? We have noting, welcoming, and then we have condemning. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was it not as equally importantly to you, the fact that they also condemned excessive force by Serbian forces against civilians and peaceful demonstrators in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, certainly. I didn't say that the Government of Serbia achieved everything from this resolution. It only started negotiations even before they were required by this resolution. So it was only the negotiations that were started before the resolution. I referred to acts of terrorism because here it says that the KLA does not hesitate to use terrorist operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Professor, regarding the question of invitations to the Albanian leaders and their failure to show up at meetings, you've told us first that you were there for it sounds like seven working days in a row between the 12th and the 20th of March. Did you go back that following week on the 23rd of March or did you give up your daily efforts to have meetings at that time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We continued sending out invitations, no longer every day. There was a rhythm, so to speak, to these invitations. There were 17, I think, or 16 such invitations and trips made to Pristina, all the way until November 1998 when these invitations were stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I have seen some of those, Professor, in the documents that were attached with your 92 ter statement, but I'm not sure I've seen 16 or 17. Do you have the entire collection of invitations that were sent out by you during that time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I reconstructed this based on my diaries. I'm sure that there's also official information about it. I have all the dates when I was in Pristina. Sometimes I went on my own without the delegation as, for example, on the 18th of August, 1998, when I sent an invitation to Mr. Fehmi Agani for the two of us to meet. So it wasn't always the entire delegation that went.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You made reference just now to your diaries. Did you refer to your diaries in preparing for your testimony this week and last?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but they were very brief, just a sentence or two. It was more to remind myself of what I was supposed to do the next day rather than recording past events. It was more of a reminder for the future rather than a description of what was passed. So when I glanced at that, I was able to reconstruct it. But in many of the books dealing with this subject matter, the dates are recorded when the delegation of the Republic of Serbia went to Pristina to negotiate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You mentioned, in connection with the invitations, that Mr. Veljko Odalovic showed you a receipt signed by Mr. Merovci who was chief of cabinet for Mr. Rugova, indicating that the invitation had been received. Do you recall, did this happen on one occasion, I take it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Odalovic once showed me that. I saw it with my own eyes. He showed this to me in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. That was in Pristina. Do you recall when that was, approximately?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't one of the first seven times. It was at a later stage, when we were beginning to wonder whether invitations were being received, especially Mr. Rugova. Mr. Odalovic was the head of the Kosovo district at the time, and he was the one who showed me this. I had asked him whether the invitations were being received regularly; and in order to document the fact that they were, he showed me Mr. Merovci's signature to the effect that Mr. Rugova's invitation had been received.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With regard to that particular one for which you saw a signed receipt, do you recall how far in advance that invitation had gone out and what the receipt date was vis-a-vis the scheduled meeting date?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to remember that sort of detail. It has been a very long time, after all. If he still has the documents in his possession, then Mr. Odalovic might be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, Professor. I just needed to ask. All right. Did you keep a record of -- well, I think you told us you weren't responsible for technical details. Did someone keep a record of when the invitations went out and by what means they were sent and to where they were sent and how far in advance they were sent? Was there some sort of log or correspondence register regarding these things?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. It's all in the possession of the Government of the Republic of Serbia. First of all, one always travelled to Pristina by plane, to Pristina and back; therefore, a plane was being used. That had to be signed for. It all had to be arranged ahead of time and prepared ahead of time. I'm quite certain that the Government of Serbia still has well-ordered files on when exactly people travelled to Pristina and who was on that plane.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know in which archive those particular records would be kept?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Secretariat of the Government of the Republic of Serbia. This is a sector attached to the government, and this sector deals precisely with these kinds of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You say, at page 13147, that in April, May, and August you went there again, I take it to Pristina, to have meetings with Mr. Fehmi Agani. Was he the only one you scheduled meetings with in April, May, and August?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I scheduled a meeting with Mr. Agani on the 18th of August. That was the only time, the 18th of August, 1998. The rest of the times there were government delegations, and invitations had been sent out to representatives of the majority Albanian -- major Albanian parties. However, the responses later came from people representing all of the ethnic communities and the two non-majority Albanian parties in Kosovo as well. We actually worked at those meetings. We got work done. We didn't go there for nothing, it's just that the majority Albanian parties were not represented.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But in April, May, and August, your invitations went out to Mr. Agani and the other heads of the major Albanian parties, Mr. Rugova, et cetera, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was just that once, on the 18th of August, that I sent an invitation to Mr. Agani. All the previous invitations were sent to Albanian political leaders and representatives of all ethnic minorities, generally speaking, and those were the people who came to those meetings. But the invitations were sent to everyone alike. I'm, in fact, quite certain that there was a meeting that took place early in June 1998, not just in May, therefore; early in June 1998 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But in April, May, and June. Invitations went out from you to Rugova and the other Kosovo Albanian leaders of the larger Albanian parties, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, in August, did you just send a single invitation to Mr. Agani or was there an invitation to all the other leaders of the major parties as well?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The invitation was sent to Mr. Agani alone. He sent me a letter as well. One can see that. This is something that we discussed some days ago, and we actually read both of the letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And you said in your testimony that there was: "Testimony by Mr. Fehmi Agani that they always received those invitations, but that they deliberately did not want to respond to them." Professor, when you say "testimony," to me that connotes testimony like yours in a courtroom somewhere. Is that what you meant? Has Mr. Agani testified about that somewhere?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I never said that. However, in his letter, he claims to have received the invitation and also confirms that he previously received all of the invitations as well. He claims that he received the invitation in relation to the 18th of June, or whatever the date was; but if you go back to the letter, you will see the exact date. He talks about a specific invitation, not about the procedure of sending out invitations in general. If I use the word "testify," I didn't imply a formal testimony. I meant he confirmed in his letter that he had received my invitation. That is what he claims in his letter. He testifies to the fact that he had received my invitation. The word "to testify" probably means more than just formally testifying in a court of law, at least in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The reference was to your testimony at page 13150, and I just wanted to be clear about that. I didn't think that he had testified in court anywhere about that. And, in his letter, he indicated that he had received invitations; but your evidence, on the 8th of August, seemed to refer to "they," and I take that meaning all the other leaders. Did he say that specifically or did you just infer that, that if he had gotten it, the others must have as well?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My conclusion was that if he had received it, why would it be different for anybody else. Let me get this straight again. This was not something Agani actually wrote in his letter. It was just my conclusion. If he had received his invitation, why would any of the others involved not receive theirs since all invitations had been sent. Mr. Agani says in his letter that he always received all of the invitations. We can bring up the letter, if you like. So instead of just interpreting what we remember about the letter, we can check his original wording.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will do that, Professor, a little later on, if you permit me. I want to go on to something else now, but I do have that farther down my list. At page 13152, Mr. Zecevic was asking you about a letter dated the 26th of April, 1998, from you to Mr. Rugova, and this is Exhibit 1D18. I'm not sure what page number it is, but I think this is tab 11 in your red binder. And I think the particular exhibit we have is actually from Professor Weller's book about Kosovo. Was the original letter in English or is that just a translation of your letter that was written in some other language?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm quite certain that the original letter was not in English. Why would it have been? Neither Mr. Agani nor I are Englishmen, are we?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. But occasionally we see some documents from the Republic of Serbia or individuals in the Serbian government where we have an original in English, and that is a question I have sometimes in those instances. The letter was dated the 26th, referring to a meeting scheduled on the 28th. Had that meeting been scheduled for some time before or is this the first setting of the meeting? The way it reads, it sounds like it was previously scheduled.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember whether it was previously scheduled this time around, but I do see that there is a meeting being scheduled for the 28th in Pristina. One thing that I find slightly strange is that no specific time is set for the meeting. We always set the time for any of the meetings. Perhaps this was the very meeting. Mr. Odalovic showed me that receipt by Mr. Merovci to the effect that he had received the letter. Maybe that was in reference to this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we expect Mr. Odalovic to come here later. Maybe we'll have a chance to ask him about it. I want to go now to May. At page 13153, at line 24, Mr. Zecevic was asking you about 22nd of May and a meeting at the headquarters of the Pristina Writers' Association. You remember that meeting, and was this the first and the only time you got the to sit down with your group and actually meet with some of the leaders of the major Kosovo Albanian parties?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was the first and only time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned in your testimony that on the other side Mr. Veton Surroi was there, Blerim Shala, Mahmut Bakalli, Mr. Kelmendi. What about anyone else? Was Mr. Rugova there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Rugova wasn't there. The only form in which he was present was his photograph on the wall of that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Was Mr. Agani there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Mr. Agani was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Do you recall if Adem Demaqi or Mr. Thaqi or Mr. Krasniqi were there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never laid eyes on Mr. Demaqi, and I saw Mr. Thaqi for the very first time when we met in Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I believe it was your testimony that you really didn't have any discussion about substance on this occasion. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. This was a discussion that was not binding for any of the parties. It was more of an introduction to future talks than a meaningful discussion in itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I seem to recall from the testimony of Mr. Surroi that, in his view, there was a little substance discussed at this meeting, but perhaps that can be just a difference in opinion on what "substance" means. And was it at this meeting that Mr. Surroi asked you if you were willing to speak to Ambassador Chris Hill, who apparently was on the premises somewhere at the time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was on the premises. Mr. Surroi asked me if I would agree, and I said I would be prepared to meet Mr. Hill any time but in Belgrade and not now because we were there on a different business. In Belgrade I said he was free to schedule an appointment with me any time. I would be glad to see him, but we were in Pristina now to talk to the Kosovo Albanian delegation rather than to Mr. Hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Prior to this May 22nd meeting, had any of the leaders of the Kosovo Albanian parties indicated their desire to have an international presence and/or participation in the negotiations with you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This request always loomed large as far as the Albanian party was concerned every time they came around to talks like these, but they kept refusing to have talks like these in Pristina and this was the reason. They were reluctant to recognise the state of Serbia or, for that mattered, to discuss the position of Kosovo and Metohija with the state of Serbia alone. They were pushing for the entire issue to be internationalised, as it were, and not to be viewed as a domestic issue for Serbia, for the Republic of Serbia, and that was the reason for their adamant refusal to hold talks in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you did not have another meeting with them, other than to the extent you had a meeting with some of them in Rambouillet and Paris later on. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were no formal meetings even in Rambouillet or in Paris. They were chance encounters when we bumped into each other or happened to be in the same room.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand your testimony about that. At this May 22nd meeting, after so many efforts on your part to try and actually meet with these guys, it seems odd to me that there wasn't a greater effort made at discussing some substance because you worked long and hard to try and get them in a room and sit down and talk to them. In your view, why was no substance, real substance, discussed at this meeting? Was that their fault, your fault, a mutual failure? How would you characterise that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, they refused to accept this very notion, the notion that there should be talks between the two delegations and that no international player was to be party to those talks or directly attend. That was probably the reason that Mr. Surroi asked me to meet and speak to Mr. Hill for something perhaps like that to be organised.
