And that is why the talks were insubstantial, so to speak, the talks on the 22nd of May. There was no real substance to them. I'm quite certain that that was the reason. Perhaps Mr. Surroi believed that the very fact that we had managed to meet and exchanged a couple of empty phrases constituted some sort of a progress; however, I believe he couldn't even tell you himself what the substance might have been of those talks or name any of the specific conclusions. I'm referring to the talks on the 22nd of May, 1998. Those were very general talks. They were not binding for either of the parties. It was quite clear at the time that there was not much chance of the talks continuing because the Albanians refused to talk directly to the delegation of the Republic of Serbia and they refused to acknowledge that the question of Kosovo was a domestic issue for the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, you were aware of the so-called St. Edigio education agreement, I think, reached sometime in September 1996?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean St. Edigio?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the substance of that agreement, as it was a member of the government and Mr. Percevic and the late Mr. Dobrosav Bjeletic who were in charge of this. I'm not aware with the substance, as I said, but I know that such talks were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand the point that you're making about the Albanian side being reluctant to travel to Belgrade for meetings and being seen as recognising the Serb government, but wasn't it expressed to you by Mr. Surroi and others that they had reluctance to negotiate without the participation of internationals because their past experience had been not very encouraging. And I point to the St. Edigio education agreement as an example. That was something that was signed by Mr. Rugova and Mr. Milosevic in September of 1996, but 18 months later in March 1998 still nothing concrete had really been done about it, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know whether anything had been done about it or not. Once when we travelled to Pristina there were two student rallies being held against us. The premises of certain universities had been handed over to the Albanians, and there was a huge uproar and riots in which some members of your delegation were injured. I received some slight injuries myself, in fact. Those were demonstrations being held in Pristina, and I can't really tell you about the pace at which the agreement was eventually implemented. I wasn't in charge of that and I didn't really keep an eye on that. By the time I got involved with the talks, the agreement had long been a matter of the past, it had been signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, the transcript didn't reflect that Professor said that those were -- it's 97, 7 and 8: "Those were demonstrations being held in Pristina by Serbian and Montenegrin students."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that what you said, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So, Professor, then I understand because of this lack of success and lack of willingness on the part of the Kosovar Albanian representatives of the major parties, you sort of went ahead then and dealt with those who were willing to meet with you, including Mr. Faik Jashari and the representatives of the Turks and Gorani and the Egyptians, correct, and some others?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At the time, do you know what the ethnic percentages were in Kosovo? Isn't it true that between the Serbs and the Albanians in Kosovo, didn't they account for the overwhelming majority of the population in Kosovo, 80 per cent, 90 per cent, between Albanians and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, but you cannot ignore the fact that apart from Serbs and Albanians there were other ethnic communities even though small, and they were as sensitive to their ethnic attributes as the major two. They had their language, their culture, their tradition. So those ethnic communities also had to be asked. They couldn't be ignored.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 98, lines 1 and 2, reference to a person "Jashari," is that the name you've been using? Is it accurately reproduced?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think, it's spelled J-a-s-a-r-i.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, can you tell us how Faik Jashari spells his last name, the one who was negotiating with you and signed the agreement in November 1998?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I don't know the Albanian language, and I don't know how it's written. I know how it's transcribed, but I don't know the spelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He was also a member of your delegation to Rambouillet, yeah?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I understand that, and that's a very difficult, sensitive, issue for anyone dealing with those matters; but, Professor, as a practical matter, how does that work? I mean, how far do you go in trying to include everybody in working out something like this? I mean, in Kosovo, if you have two Azerbaijanis willing to participate in the process, isn't there some limit where you can say, Sorry, you're not substantially significant enough number-wise to participate in this process. We can't allow people two people to nullify what the other 99.7 percentage of us want to do.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a factual issue, and I believe that in those proposals for self-government in Kosovo and Metohija we had established a kind of lower threshold. At any rate, the presence of those ethnic communities -- I'm not sure I'll get the number right, but I believe there were around 600.000 non-Albanians. That's the figure that circulated at the time. We can check it in the census. But the Serbian ethnic community was very strong --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The Turkish ethnic community was very strong.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Textbooks used to be printed in Turkish, and I believe they still are. Kosovo and Metohija was for centuries part of the Ottoman Empire under Turkish rule, and that would have meant an infraction of minority rights not to include them. That's what they emphasised, too. The issue of Kosovo and Metohija is not only an issue between Serbs and Albanians. They said, We too should have a say in determining the future order in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see at page 99, line 17, you indicated you thought there were around 600.000 non-Albanians in Kosovo. Is that correct.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the figure that was accepted at the time. I'm not sure. As you know, there were no formal censuses. That's the figure that circulated at the time. It was mentioned in several sources, in books, in the press, and other media. It was said that that was the ratio; 600.000 including Serbs, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Do you know how many of that 600.000 non-Albanians would have been Serbs, half or more?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, anything I say would be speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How can I speak about numbers without having the census?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It was only if you knew. Don't speculate, please. Now, I'm coming to the point you mentioned before. You had a communication with Fehmi Agani in August, and I think that was Exhibit 1D600. I'm not sure what tab number that is. Professor, I will see if I can find it for you. No, maybe I've written it down wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Zecevic can help us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here, I found it. It's tab 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, it's 1D064 is the exhibit number and 1D061 appears to be your letter to him and 1D064 is his response. Could we look at 1D061 first, which is tab 17, Professor, I think, according to my list. Is that your invitation to Mr. Agani?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and we see precisely that the invitation was addressed only to Mr. Agani.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, in the, letter you propose that you meet the next day, the 18th of August, at 2.00 in the afternoon. Could we go to the other exhibit, 1D064. This seems to be a press release about that letter. Professor, do you recall seeing in your binder the letter that Mr. Agani had written to you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's tab 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Tab 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Of the red binder?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Of the red binder, 1D64.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Isn't that the one we have up now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That I think is tab 17.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 17 is my letter, but the letter of Mr. Agani's tab 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is the one that is on the e-court that's tab 16, 1D64, letter from Mr. Agani to Professor Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I see on the screen before me now that a letter in English, Professor, is from Dr. Agani addressed to you saying: "We received your letter. We also want negotiations." And the last sentence says: "I hope that Ambassador Hill, who is in constant contact with Belgrade and Pristina, will help determine the exact manner and time for continuance of the negotiations." But when you wrote back in response to that letter, you made no mention of Ambassador Hill and you simply suggested that Dr. Agani meet with you on the 18th. Did you -- did you do that on purpose, neglect to mention Mr. Hill? You just want him involved, did you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to talk with Mr. Agani, obviously. Since Ambassador Hill is not mentioned, I can only guess. Mr. Agani did not respond to the invitation. At that time I wasn't clear on the status of Ambassador Hill. I did not understand his role in the negotiations between the delegation of the government and Kosovo Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But in your reply to Dr. Agani, you didn't ask him about what he meant by Ambassador Hill being in contact with Belgrade and how he might fit in and why Mr. Agani suggested that he be involved; you just ignored him, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Ambassador Hill?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I ignored him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps this would be a good time for the break for the day. I anticipate I'll be finished before lunch tomorrow. I don't know if I'll finish by the end of the first session but hopefully by lunchtime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. End of the day, Professor. We will continue, as usual, tomorrow at 9.00. You may now leave the courtroom with the usher, and we shall see you then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 14th day of August, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24
